newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam makes room for currency to slide.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam makes room for currency to slide.

text.p: Vietnam bowed to persistent selling pressure against its currency on Monday, prising open the official interbank trading band to make room for a slide in the direction of much lower black market rates.
As the country's embryonic foreign exchange market digested the unexpected news, central State Bank of Vietnam Governor Cao Si Kiem moved to head off talk of devaluation.
"I would like to emphasise once more that the State Bank's view is that there should be no devaluation of the Vietnam dong," he told the official Dau Tu newspaper.
He stressed that monetary policy was aimed at managing the currency in line with market supply and demand, controlling imports, encouraging exports and promoting economic stability.
He also underlined the need for currency stability, which has become a constant refrain in official circles since economic reforms brought an end to hyperinflation in the late 1980s.
A State Bank official told Reuters that the trading band for the dong had been widened to five percent on either side of the daily official rate from one percent.
In one stroke, that gave the dong room to drop almost four percent from last week's level of around 11,208 per U.S. dollar.
The official rate was set at 11,096 per dollar on Monday, which put the new floor at 11,650 and the ceiling at 10,542.
The dong's stability at about 11,000 per dollar since 1994, combined with high inflation, led to a real appreciation of about 10 percent against currencies of Vietnam's main trading partners.

The currency's fading competitiveness came under scrutiny last year as exports slowed and imports took off -- Vietnam notched up a record trade deficit of $4.0 billion in 1996, equivalent to 18 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP).
After much debate, the authorities decided against a sudden devaluation and opted for a policy of gradual depreciation.
Since November, the State Bank has allowed the dong to ease, first by doubling the fluctuation band to plus/minus one percent and then by pegging its pivot rate lower every week.
However, the depreciation has not been fast enough for a market hungry for dollars.

While the dong languished on its interbank market floor, it traded actively at much lower rates in the streets. Traders said it was changing hands at around 11,550 per dollar on the black market on Monday and had been as low as 11,850 last month.
Deputy Trade Minister Mai Van Dau told Dau Tu that Vietnam should not rely on a depreciation of its currency to help sell its goods abroad.
However, he spoke in favour of allowing supply and demand to determine the exchange rate, adding: "The black market rate has reflected the demand-supply situation quite correctly over the last year."
Kiem said deadlines for payment on a rash of letters of credit, which were issued last year for imports, had bolstered demand for dollars.
Questions about the financial health of the country's nascent banking system were raised last week following a report that one privately held bank had defaulted on a deferred letter of credit.
